sao-francisco.name: Church of Saint Francis
sao-francisco.short: A Franciscan convent with a 15th-century Gothic apse, a rebuilt hall-nave and the tomb of Constança de Noronha
sao-francisco.long: The Franciscans reached Guimarães in 1217 with Friar Gualter, sent by Francis of Assisi himself. Their first convent by the town walls was demolished in 1325 by order of King Dinis, so that it would not compromise the town's defence. The present convent was founded in 1400 at the wish of João I; the Gothic apse was finished around 1461. In the 1740s the nave was turned into a single hall by removing the columns and arches and was enriched with gilded altarpieces. Constança de Noronha, first Duchess of Bragança, is buried in the church.
sao-francisco.history:
The Franciscan story in Guimarães begins in 1217, when Friar Gualter arrived in Portugal, sent by Francis of Assisi to establish the Order of Friars Minor here. Gualter settled in Guimarães; after a first, very precarious period, the friars took over a hospice by the town walls in 1271 and built a convent beside it. From the outset they clashed with the collegiate church of Guimarães, which tried to keep the order out of the town.

The convent by the walls did not last long: in 1325 King Dinis ordered it demolished, because in a siege the friars' fortifications threatened the town's security. The friars moved into makeshift houses and stayed there until 1400, when João I ordered the convent rebuilt on the site it still occupies. The work lasted through much of the 15th century; the Gothic apse was finished around 1461. That same year Constança de Noronha (1395–1480), first Duchess of Bragança, joined the Third Order of Saint Francis and asked to be buried in this church. Her tomb with its recumbent effigy can still be seen inside.

A cloister in the classical, Mannerist taste survives from the end of the 16th century — an important work of its time. But the great early-modern remodelling came in the 1740s, when the nave was completely altered: the arches and columns were removed to create a single, unified “hall church” (igreja-salão). The three original arches between the transept and the nave were replaced by a single monumental arch. At the same time the new high altarpiece by Miguel Francisco da Silva was installed, executed by Manuel da Costa Andrade, along with many gilded side altarpieces.

From the Middle Ages the chancel survives above all: a large polygonal apse flanked by two smaller apsidioles. The windows of the apse, with their colonnettes and mouldings, and the carving of the capitals, show the influence of the monastery of Batalha. Inside, both the chancel and the side parts of the chevet are covered by ribbed vaults. The main portal of the church and the chapter-house portal in the cloister are also Gothic, though in its blunt simplicity the main portal looks more like Romanesque work.

The building was protected in stages: the frescoes were listed in 1940, the apse and apsidioles in 1953, and in 1974 the cloister and the Baroque building of the Third Order were added, together with the 18th-century sacristy. In 2009 the remains and relics of São Gualter were rediscovered in the convent church, hidden inside an old processional image.

The main portal, despite its Gothic dating, looks almost Romanesque, while the apse with its tall windows recalls the influence of Batalha; together these details make the church a kind of textbook of Portuguese church architecture from Gothic to Baroque. The convent is still an important centre of the Franciscan tradition in Guimarães, with an active parish and Third Order. The church was restored in the 20th century, which recovered some of the interior's original character, but it also keeps its 18th-century Baroque altarpieces. Next to it lies the Couros tanning quarter, along the stream where hides were worked from the 13th century; church and quarter together form one of the most coherent corners of the old town and part of the UNESCO World Heritage site.

sao-francisco.tip: This is a working parish church; entry is usually free, but the doors may be shut at midday, so check the times on the spot. Look at the Gothic apse from outside, the main portal, the Baroque hall interior and the cloister with its chapter house. The church stands on Largo de São Francisco, next to the Couros tanning quarter; it pairs well with a walk through the Couros Zone and along Avenida Alberto Sampaio.
